children: Foreign policy may be one of the biggest, and more understated, issues driving voters to the polls today. The Iran war and tariffs, for instance, are inextricably tied into many people's perceptions of the economy — for better or worse.
But the results are unlikely to fundamentally redirect U.S. foreign policy, even if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Many of President Donald Trump's most divisive policies, including tariffs, immigration enforcement and military actions, have been driven largely by executive authority. And some broader strategic objectives, such as securing access to critical minerals and reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese supply chains, have bipartisan support.

Congress could theoretically constrain the executive branch by passing legislation limiting the president's authority. But even if Democrats win control of the Senate, they are unlikely to secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster and advance most legislation. And if the president vetoes that legislation, lawmakers would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override the veto. Democrats are unlikely to secure the seats needed to reach that threshold.

Over the past four decades, Congress has rarely managed to override presidential vetoes on matters touching on foreign policy, underscoring the difficulty of using legislation to rein in the White House, says James Lindsay, senior fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations.
Without a congressional supermajority, Democrats will be constrained, but not crippled.

Dawson Law, founder of geopolitical advisory Conseil Global Advisors, expects they will likely ramp up scrutiny of the administration, which means subpoenas, requests for information, and many congressional hearings that "will very much touch the foreign policy world." They will likely touch the business world too, with Democrats taking a closer look at deals struck by the Trump administration both domestically and abroad.
Companies or any other third-party entities who have struck deals with the government could be made to testify as well, Law says.

Democrats could also use defense spending as leverage. The administration requested $1.15 trillion in base discretionary appropriations for defense for fiscal 2027 plus an extra $350 billion in reconciliation funding and about $70 billion to cover some of the costs of the Iran war.

The government's current funding measure expires in December, and sitting lawmakers will have to decide whether they pass a full-year appropriations bill or another short-term continuing resolution that will punt the decision until after new members of congress get sworn in January. If Democrats take either chamber, they're likely to wait, and could negotiate the amount of defense spending down.

Perhaps more important is how Trump reacts to the added congressional scrutiny. In fact, the second half of his administration "is likely to be even more disruptive" than the first, CFR's Lindsay says. The U.S. resumed limited "defensive" strikes on Iran Monday evening even as peace negotiations remain under way.
Byron Callan, an analyst at Capital Alpha Partners, agrees.

"We don't expect Trump to offer conciliatory messages of cooperation with Congress or that he will change his views on Executive Privilege," he writes. "He could become more combative on defense and security issues in late 2026 and in 2027-28."
